newsitem.title: POLAND: FOCUS-POLAND'S GRAIN QUALITY HIT BY FLOODS.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-POLAND'S GRAIN QUALITY HIT BY FLOODS.

text.p: July's catastrophic floods and bad weather have not diminished Polish grain output as much as earlier expected but affected the quality of the grain, which could set off some imports, analysts said on Wednesday.

The Central Statistical Office (GUS) estimated that this year's grain harvest should be 24.5-24.8 million tonnes against 24.9 million tonnes last year. Previous preliminary Agriculture Ministry estimates were more pessimistic at 24 million tonnes.
"In a nutshell, there is a lot of grain this year but its quality is low," Henryk Hinc, the head of the state's grain warehouse firm PZZ told Reuters.

In reaction to lower grain quality the state's food market regulator, the Farm Market Agency (ARR) on Tuesday lowered quality requirements for grain purchased from farmers, a move which may further reduce the attributes of Poland's crop.

The ARR decreased the Hagberg falling time from 200 to 170 seconds on grain bought from farmers along with lowering the parameter of gluten solubility while leaving gluten content, contamination level and grain equalization unchanged.

"Such lower quality grain will be more difficult to store, potentially increasing storage losses, and may not meet technological norms for bread production," Jadwiga Rothkaehl of the Central Laboratory of Grain Processing and Storage said.

"Storing the lower quality grain will be more difficult especially because a large portion of Poland's warehouses do not have separate containers for different quality grain...so high quality grain may suffer if grains are mixed," she said.
But the ARR said that even with its lower requirements, all grain bought by the agency would meet consumption norms.
"These lower requirements are still within the second class of Polish norms -- grain adequate for bread and consumption," ARR spokesman Stanislaw Myslinski told Reuters.
Until Tuesday the ARR bought some 9,300 tonnes of wheat and 6,500 tonnes of rye to replenish its reserves from the planned 190,000 tonnes and 65,000 tonnes respectively.
ARR authorised private warehouses have so far bought 2,831 tonnes of wheat and 4,800 tonnes of rye from a planned overall total of 1.75 million tonnes for all grain types.
Some analysts questioned whether GUS's harvest estimates, based on average yields of 28.2-28.6 quintals per hectare or some 97.6-98.9 percent of last year's results, were overly optimistic.
"This may be overestimated, 28 quintals is slightly too much even though northern regions will have banner harvests," said Piotr Beska, analyst at food trader Eternus.

GUS said the total grain losses from the flooding and bad weather which hit southern and western part of the country last month could amount to 1.4-1.7 million tonnes, of which 0.5-0.7 million tonnes were directly a result of the flooding.
Analysts said, however, that while the grain losses were not high enough to spark largescale imports, the drop of its quality could trigger imports if the damage was widespread.
"As for today, imports can be considered merely as a means to upgrade grain quality, but this depends on its quality throughout the country," a Warsaw based grain analyst said.

The country's Meteorology and Water Management Institute (IMGW) has said that crop conditions in early August remained slightly below corresponding 1996 levels, but did not deteriorate further after last month's flooding.

The ministry's spokesperson Malgorzta Ksiazek earlier said that Poland would import the usual 400,000-600,000 tonnes of high-gluten durum wheat in the 1997/98 season and that needs of further imports would only be known after the harvest ends.
Poland, whose growing season runs from September to August, does not grow some types of high-gluten grains and therefore imports them every year.
Last month's floods submerged a total of 6,600 sq km, or nearly two percent of Poland's surface area, killed 54 and forced tens thousands out of their homes, causing damage of billions of dollars.
